The figure above shows the graph of a function $y=f(x)$ and its inverse $y={f}^{-1}(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(2,1)$ and lies on $y=f(x).$ The point $B$ has coordinates $(1,2)$ and lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$ If ${f}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4},$ what is $({f}^{-1})^{′}(1)?$

$({f}^{-1})^{′}(1)=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Since $B\,(1,2)$ lies on ${f}^{-1},$ we have ${f}^{-1}(1)=2.$
We're also told that ${f}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Evaluating at $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4})} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
